options: Skipping micro-partitions whose min/max metadata shows they cannot match the filter

challenges.title: Sales analytics with window functions
challenges.prompt: Write three analytics queries over a small sales table: monthly revenue with a running total and share of region, the best rep per region and the month-over-month change. These run on PostgreSQL here because Snowflake is not available to me; the SQL is standard, and where Snowflake offers QUALIFY the comments say so.
challenges.starter:
create table sales(id int, region text, rep text, sold_on date, amount numeric);
insert into sales values
 (1,'north','ana','2026-01-05',120),(2,'north','bo','2026-01-09',80),(3,'north','ana','2026-02-02',200),
 (4,'south','cy','2026-01-07',150),(5,'south','di','2026-01-20',90),(6,'south','cy','2026-02-11',60),
 (7,'north','bo','2026-02-15',140),(8,'south','di','2026-02-28',300);

-- TODO 1: monthly revenue per region (to_char(sold_on,'YYYY-MM')) with a running total per region and each month's % of the region total (1 decimal); order by region, month
-- TODO 2: the best rep per region by total amount (ties by rep name) - Snowflake would use QUALIFY; here use a subquery with row_number()
-- TODO 3: month-over-month change in revenue per region using lag(); the first month's change is NULL (printed as empty)
challenges.explain: Window functions can wrap aggregates (sum(sum(amount)) over ...), and row_number() in a subquery is exactly what QUALIFY expresses in Snowflake. lag() gives the previous month, NULL for the first. Verified by running it on PostgreSQL 18; not run on Snowflake.

challenges.title: An idempotent change-capture upsert
challenges.prompt: Simulate a stream plus MERGE: find the new and changed staging rows, apply them to the target only when values really differ and prove a second run finds nothing left to do. PostgreSQL's ON CONFLICT stands in for Snowflake's MERGE; Snowflake itself was not used.
challenges.explain: IS DISTINCT FROM compares row values null-safely, so unchanged rows are not rewritten and the pending count drops to zero. In Snowflake you would write MERGE INTO ... WHEN MATCHED AND (...) THEN UPDATE WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT. Verified by running it on PostgreSQL 18; not run on Snowflake.
